notes:
Need to search first.I couldn't finish all three parts. I ran out of search and fetch calls partway through, so the notes below rely on only a few pages. **Part 1 (the traditional reading)** is reasonably well covered. **Parts 2 and 3 are mostly missing.** I didn't reach any site run by a particular church tradition (Reformed, Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Lutheran, Catholic or Orthodox), or bibleodyssey.org. I also couldn't open netbible.org directly; NET notes only appear where preceptaustin quotes them. Where commentators disagree, I give the disagreement but only label a tradition when the page itself does. Verses with nothing are left out (v. 13 and v. 24 have no separate notes).

**Main sources used**
- Enduring Word (David Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/
- Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm (the part I read covers about vv. 1–12)
- Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary
- Constable's Notes: https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-28.html
- bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-28

---

**v. 1**
- The sailors probably knew Malta but not this side of it, because nearly all ships used the main port on the far side. The name may mean "honey" if it comes from Greek, or "refuge" if it comes from the Phoenician language. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/
- Ellicott says this is clearly modern Malta, the only island the Greeks and Romans called Melita. He rejects the alternative, Meleda in the Adriatic Sea, as having no real evidence behind it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary also says Malta, not Meleda. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-28.html
- Precept Austin reads "brought safely through" as a "divine passive": God saved them, as His angel had promised, not the sailors' skill. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary

**v. 2**
- The Greek literally says "no common kindness." The word for "received" means both shelter and hospitality. The cold shows the wind was not the hot sirocco. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm
- The word "barbarians" (KJV) was not an insult. It just meant people who didn't speak Greek or Latin. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-28
- Guzik notes Luke writes as an eyewitness of both the kindness and the cold. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/

**v. 3**
- Paul gathering sticks shows a servant's heart and humility. Doing good brought out the viper, but Paul stayed calm. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/ ; https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-28
- Matthew Henry: Paul was willing to do humble tasks. We should think nothing beneath us except sin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_028.cfm
- The viper was probably asleep for the winter and woke up in the heat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/28-1.htm ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-28.html
- **Was the snake really poisonous?** Commentators disagree:
  - Barclay (labelled "Presbyterian · Calvinism" on StudyLight) can't say whether this was a miracle. He notes Malta has no poisonous snakes today and that in Paul's time there was a harmless look-alike. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/28-3.html
  - Coffman, on the same page, is impatient with Ramsay for calling the snake "harmless." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/28-3.html
  - Ellicott, the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary and Constable all say vipers simply died out on Malta later as the island was farmed and filled up. Ellicott also says the Greek word for "sticks" fits the thorny heather still found near the bay. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-28.html ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-28.html
- **Did it actually bite him?** The Greek word can mean bit or coiled around (bible.org). A Bible Hub commentator says a bite is clearly implied and it's hard to believe a viper would cling without biting. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-28 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/28-3.htm
- Kelly sees here a fulfilment of one of the promises in the disputed ending of Mark (Mark 16:18). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/28-3.html

**v. 4**
- "Justice" is a goddess (Dikē). The islanders knew Paul was a prisoner and assumed he had committed a terrible crime that the goddess would not let go unpunished. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary (quoting the NET note and Larkin on the islanders' animistic worldview)
- Ellicott: the islanders' rough sense of God's justice made them jump to a conclusion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm
- Gill: they may have seen his chain. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/28-4.html
- Calvin: the islanders went wrong by judging Paul without knowing his life and by not waiting to see the outcome. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/28-4.html
- Clarke doubts the snake really bit him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/28-4.html
- bible.org compares the irony to Amos 5:19. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-28
- One Bible Hub writer notes that even these islanders had consciences that knew of divine punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/28-1.htm

**v. 5**
- God hadn't saved Paul from the storm only to let a snake kill him. The promise that he would reach Rome (Acts 23:11) still stood. Guzik adds that God's justice has no claim on anyone whose sins Christ has paid for. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/
- Henry applies it to us: when we ignore people's slanders and keep a clear conscience, we "shake off the viper." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_028.cfm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/28-3.htm
- Fortner: God used the viper to make people take notice of Paul. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/28-5.html

**v. 6**
- The word for "swell up" means inflammation. The islanders may have thought of gods like Apollo or Asclepius, who were shown overcoming snakes. Ellicott calls it the reverse of what happened at Lystra in Acts 14. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm
- Bengel notes how fickle human opinion is: Paul is either a murderer or a god. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary
- Guzik: Paul was neither, so be careful about what others think of you. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/
- bible.org: it shows the islanders were superstitious and worshipped many gods. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-28

**v. 7**
- "Chief man" (literally "first man") was the official title of the island's Roman officer. Inscriptions on Malta confirm it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary (NET note and Gilbrant) ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/ (quoting Boice on Luke's accuracy)
- Ellicott: Publius probably hosted only a few, not all 276. Notice v. 2 says "all" and v. 7 doesn't. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm
- Lowell Johnson thinks Publius provided for all 276. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-acts-lowell-johnson

**v. 8**
- Luke uses exact medical words. The plural "fevers" suggests a fever that kept coming back. Praying and then laying on hands recalls James 5:14–15, and coming right after the snakebite it recalls Mark 16:18. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm
- Some identify the illness as "Malta fever," caught from goats' milk. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/
- Precept Austin: Paul prayed first, then acted, which is an example for us. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary
- The laying on of hands is described as a "means" (Clarke) and as a "sign" (Gill). https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/acts/28-8.html
- A Bible Hub study note says the healing proved Paul was a true apostle (2 Cor 12:12). https://biblehub.com/acts/28-8.htm

**v. 9**
- **Were the others healed by miracle or by medicine?** Guzik says the word for "healed" here can mean receiving medical treatment, so Luke the doctor may have worked as a medical missionary. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/
- By contrast, Ellicott pictures all the island's sick rushing to use Paul's healing power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm
- Constable says the Holy Spirit included these healings to show God's power still worked through Paul, though Paul could heal only those God wanted healed. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-28.html

**v. 10**
- The word "honours" was also used for a doctor's fee, which fits Luke's profession. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm
- Constable: Paul served God and both the islanders and Paul were blessed (Matt 6:33; Phil 4:19). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-28.html

**v. 11**
- Castor and Pollux (the "Heavenly Twins") were the ship's guardian gods and the gods of sailors. Seeing their stars was a good omen. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary (NET note) ; https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=act&chapter=28&verse=11
- They sailed earlier than usual. A ship from Alexandria wintering there fits Malta, which lay on the normal route. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm

**v. 12**
- Syracuse was a famous city of Sicily, about 80–100 miles away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/28.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/

**v. 14**
- Puteoli had a Jewish community, so a church there is not surprising. "And so we came to Rome" shows Luke's eagerness even with about 130 miles still to go. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-28.html

**v. 15**
- The Forum of Appius was about 43 miles from Rome. Going out to meet Paul was how an arriving emperor was welcomed. These believers also show the gospel reached Rome before Paul did (Bruce, Horton). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary (NET note)
- Gilbrant: even mature believers need fellowship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary

**v. 16**
- Paul was under house arrest, lightly chained to a soldier, and the guards changed regularly. That gave him a captive audience (Phil 1:13). Jesus' promise that Paul would bear witness in Rome is fulfilled. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/

**vv. 17–20**
- Paul goes "to the Jew first," as he always did. He makes several points: he is innocent; the Romans wanted to free him; he has no counter-charge against his nation; and he is chained for the Messiah, "the hope of Israel." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-28.html

**vv. 21–22**
- No letters had come, which may mean Paul's accusers knew their case was hopeless. The Roman Jewish leaders deserve credit for wanting to hear Paul himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/

**v. 23**
- Paul spent a whole day showing from the Old Testament how it points to Jesus. The kingdom he preached was spiritual, not political. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/
- Precept Austin links "persuading" to Luke 16:31, where those who won't listen to Moses and the Prophets won't be persuaded. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary

**vv. 25–27**
- The Greek word for "disagreed" means "out of tune," like jarring sounds. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary
- **Judicial hardening:** Precept Austin, citing Criswell, says God foresaw the rejection, and preaching the truth itself brought a hardening as judgment, though a believing remnant remains. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary
- Guzik stresses the human side instead: people reject the gospel because they don't want to turn and be healed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/

**v. 28**
- Paul had said this twice before (Acts 13:46; 18:6). Clarke says he speaks more firmly now. Bengel notes he said it in Asia, Greece and finally Italy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/28-28.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/28-28.htm
- Calvin: the Jews can't complain when Gentiles take the place they gave up. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/28-28.html
- Gill: Gentiles not only hear but obey and keep the faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/28-28.htm
- The Geneva Bible note: the unbelief of "the reprobate" can't cancel God's truth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/28-28.htm
- Ellicott points to Romans 9–11 for Paul's feelings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/28-28.htm
- Contending for the Faith calls this the Jews' "final rejection." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/28-28.html
- Guzik warns that judgment came on Jerusalem soon after (AD 70). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/
- Constable instead says Paul kept welcoming both Jews and Gentiles. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-28.html
- I didn't find these commentators directly debating whether this is a permanent turning from Israel.

**v. 29**
- The CSB footnote says only "some manuscripts" include this verse. https://www.blueletterbible.org/csb/act/28/31/s_1046031/
- Guzik and Henry comment on it as part of the text. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/28-28.html

**v. 30**
- The two years were probably caused by a backlog of court cases (Bruce). Paul probably paid rent by making tents. Onesimus was one of the visitors. Ephesians, Philippians and Colossians probably come from this time. Guzik thinks Paul was likely freed and later executed under Nero around AD 66–67. He suggests Acts doesn't report the trial because it was written as background for Paul's case. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/
- Constable sets the ending against what we know of Paul's later travels. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-28.html

**v. 31**
- "Unhindered" ends the book: chains can't stop God's word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-28/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-28-commentary (NET note)
- The ending points to the opportunity among the Gentiles and to Paul's boldness as an example for the church. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-28.html
- Constable also says Luke shaped the voyage to echo Jonah, whose journey also brought salvation to Gentiles. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-28.html

---

**Still to research** (in a new session):
- The tradition-specific sites (ligonier, desiringgod, ag.org, lcms, seedbed), especially on vv. 8–9 (are healing gifts for today?) and v. 28 (Israel and the church).
- Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org).
- bibleodyssey.org and netbible.org's own notes, especially on v. 29 and on why Acts ends where it does.
- Popular modern teaching (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace): nothing found yet.
